entry.issue: In a federal habeas challenge based on false testimony, must the petitioner show that the prosecutor knew the testimony was false, or is it enough to show the testimony was false and material?

sides.position: The petitioner must show that the prosecution knowingly used perjured or false testimony; without state involvement or knowledge, there is no constitutional violation.
cases: Smith, 358 F.2d 683 (cited in Marcy)
United States v. Jones, 614 F.2d 80 (5th Cir. 1980)
Burks v. Egeler, 512 F.2d 221 (6th Cir. 1975)
United States ex rel. Burnett v. Illinois, 619 F.2d 668 (7th Cir. 1980)
Lindhorst v. United States, 658 F.2d 598 (8th Cir. 1981)
Graham v. Wilson, 828 F.2d 656 (10th Cir. 1987)
Marcy v. Superintendent Phoenix SCI, 110 F.4th 210 (3d Cir. 2024)

sides.position: A constitutional violation can be found without evidence that the prosecutor knew the testimony was false (the Sanders panel's rule).
cases: Sanders (as described in Marcy; full citation not given in excerpts)

opinions.cite: Joseph Marcy v. Superintendent Phoenix SCI, 110 F.4th 210 (3rd Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: The Third Circuit requires proof that the prosecution knowingly used the false testimony, and it rejects Marcy's contrary position.
opinions.quote: And they place Marcy on the wrong side of an eightto-two circuit split.

entry.issue: Does an appeal or collateral-attack waiver in a plea agreement bar a post-conviction challenge to a § 924(c) conviction based on a predicate offense later held invalid under Johnson and Davis, where the record shows another valid predicate?

sides.position: An appeal or collateral-attack waiver does not bar a Davis challenge to a § 924(c) conviction resting on an invalid predicate, at least where the defendant makes a cognizable claim of actual innocence and enforcing the waiver would be a miscarriage of justice.
cases: United States v. McKinney, 60 F.4th 188 (4th Cir. 2023)

sides.position: An appeal or collateral-attack waiver bars a Davis challenge to a § 924(c) conviction based on a predicate invalidated by Johnson and Davis, even though the conviction may be legally invalid.
cases: King v. United States, 41 F.4th 1363 (11th Cir. 2022)
Portis v. United States, 33 F.4th 331 (6th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Goodall, 21 F.4th 555 (9th Cir. 2021)

opinions.cite: Cook v. United States, 111 F.4th 237 (2d Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: As Judge Robinson notes, multiple circuits have split on this question.

entry.issue: In AEDPA habeas review of an ineffective-assistance claim, does doubly deferential review under Strickland and 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d) apply at both the performance and prejudice steps, or only at the performance step?

sides.position: Doubly deferential review applies at both Strickland steps: AEDPA deference to the state court and deference to counsel both apply to the prejudice inquiry as well as the performance inquiry.
cases: Cullen v. Pinholster, 563 U.S. 170 (2011)

sides.position: Deference to counsel applies only at the performance step, not the prejudice step, though AEDPA deference to the state court applies at both steps.

opinions.cite: Englert v. Lowerre, 115 F.4th 69 (2d Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: In Waiters v. Lee, 857 F.3d 466 (2d Cir. 2017), this court observed that it is an “open question” in this circuit whether double deference applies at both steps of Strickland analysis, id. at 477 n.20, and that while Cullen v. Pinholster, 563 U.S. at 202, appears to support an affirmative answer, circuit courts are divided on the question.

entry.issue: Can a federal district court substitute the Crime Victims Fund as the payee of a restitution order after the judgment has become final, when the named victim has died?

sides.position: Substituting the Crime Victims Fund as restitution payee is permissible in some circumstances.
cases: United States v. Johnson, 378 F.3d 230 (2d Cir. 2004)
United States v. Hankins, 858 F.3d 1273 (9th Cir. 2017)

sides.position: Substituting the Crime Victims Fund as restitution payee is not permissible.
cases: United States v. Pawlinski, 374 F.3d 536 (7th Cir. 2004)
United States v. Speakman, 594 F.3d 1165 (10th Cir. 2010)

opinions.cite: United States v. John Jerome O'Hara, No. 23-5720 (6th Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: We take no position on if or when it is appropriate to substitute the Crime Victims Fund as the payee, which is currently the subject of a circuit split.

entry.issue: Must a court apply the rule of lenity before deferring to an agency's interpretation of an ambiguous criminal-law provision, such as a Sentencing Guidelines enhancement?

sides.position: Lenity trumps agency deference: a court must resolve genuine ambiguity in a criminal text in the defendant's favor before reaching deference (the Sixth Circuit position is reflected only in a concurrence).
cases: Cargill v. Garland, 57 F.4th 447 (5th Cir. 2023) (en banc)
United States v. Campbell, 22 F.4th 438 (4th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Phifer, 909 F.3d 372 (11th Cir. 2018)
Carter v. Welles-Bowen Realty, Inc., 736 F.3d 722 (6th Cir. 2013) (Sutton, C.J., concurring)

sides.position: Agency deference controls even where a criminal provision is ambiguous; the court defers to an anti-defendant reading of the Guidelines enhancement without first applying lenity.
cases: United States v. James Chandler, 114 F.4th 240 (3d Cir. 2024)

opinions.cite: United States v. James Chandler, 114 F.4th 240 (3rd Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: Panel majority (in this case) took the deference side, holding agency deference trumps lenity. This opinion, which is a dissent, would side with lenity and says the panel holding 'put us on the wrong side of a circuit split.' The opinion also notes that Loper Bright overruled Chevron, but it does not address whether lenity yields to Kisor deference, so the conflict as framed here appears unresolved.
opinions.quote: That holding put us on the wrong side of a circuit split.

entry.issue: Under the robbery physical-restraint enhancement in U.S.S.G. § 2B3.1(b)(4)(B), what conduct is enough to show physical restraint, such as ordering victims to lie down or threatening them with a gun, and what test should decide it?

sides.position: Physical restraint can be shown by coercive control such as gunpoint commands to lie on the floor or threats that keep victims from moving, and the enhancement was affirmed on those facts.
cases: United States v. Howell, 17 F.4th 673 (6th Cir. 2021)
United States v. Miera, 539 F.3d 1232 (10th Cir. 2008)

sides.position: Whether physical restraint applies is decided by weighing five factors: use of physical force, exerting control over the victim, providing no alternative but compliance, focusing on the victim for some period, and placement in a confined space.
cases: United States v. Bell, 947 F.3d 49 (3d Cir. 2020)

opinions.cite: United States v. Joseph Deleon, 116 F.4th 1260 (11th Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: As the circuit split deepens on the proper interpretation of the physical-restraint enhancement, Deleon’s case provides a good opportunity to reexamine our jurisprudence.

entry.issue: May the government withhold the third-level acceptance-of-responsibility motion under U.S.S.G. § 3E1.1(b) because the defendant in good faith objects to factual assertions in the presentence report or refuses to waive appeal rights?

sides.position: The government may not withhold the § 3E1.1(b) motion based on the defendant's refusal to waive appeal rights (Divens) or a good-faith objection to presentence report factual assertions (Lee).
cases: United States v. Divens, 650 F.3d 343 (4th Cir. 2011)
United States v. Lee, 653 F.3d 170 (2d Cir. 2011)

sides.position: The government has broad discretion to withhold the § 3E1.1(b) motion for any reason that does not violate the Constitution, including litigating contested relevant conduct at sentencing, which is a legitimate governmental interest.
cases: United States v. Deberry (7th Cir.)
United States v. Nurek, 578 F.3d 624 (7th Cir. 2009)
United States v. Sainz-Preciado, 566 F.3d 713 (7th Cir. 2009)
United States v. Davis, 714 F.3d 474 (7th Cir. 2013)
United States v. Lafiamma Orona, 118 F.4th 858 (7th Cir. 2024)

opinions.cite: United States v. Lafiamma Orona, 118 F.4th 858 (7th Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: Adheres to the Deberry line: Nurek and Sainz-Preciado remain binding, so objecting to relevant conduct is a legitimate basis for withholding the motion. Amendment 775 abrogated Deberry only on the appeal-waiver point and did not clearly displace Nurek and Sainz-Preciado.
opinions.quote: After our decisions in Deberry, Nurek, and Sainz-Preciado, a circuit split emerged on the scope of the government's discretion under § 3E1.1(b).

entry.issue: Does a district court impermissibly delegate its Article III sentencing authority to the probation officer when a supervised-release condition requires mental-health treatment but does not specify whether it must be inpatient or outpatient?

sides.position: No impermissible delegation: leaving the inpatient-versus-outpatient choice to the probation officer does not improperly delegate judicial authority.
cases: United States v. Aguilar-Cerda, 27 F.4th 1093 (5th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Cutler, 259 F. App'x 883 (7th Cir. 2008)

sides.position: Impermissible delegation: a district court may not let the probation officer decide whether inpatient treatment is required.
cases: United States v. Matta, 777 F.3d 116 (2d Cir. 2015)

opinions.cite: United States v. Eric Vaughn, 119 F.4th 1084 (6th Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: and circuits are split on this inpatient-outpatient claim, compare United States v. Aguilar-Cerda, 27 F.4th 1093, 1095–96 (5th Cir. 2022) (finding no impermissible delegation), and United States v. Cutler, 259 F. App’x 883, 886–87 (7th Cir. 2008) (same), with United States v. Matta, 777 F.3d 116, 122–23 (2d Cir. 2015) (finding impermissible delegation).

entry.issue: Does a private party's hash-value match of a file count as a private search, so that law enforcement may later view the matched file without a warrant?

sides.position: Yes. A hash-value match is a valid private search, so law enforcement may later view the matched file without a warrant under the private-search doctrine. Hash matching is nearly perfectly accurate and reveals nothing the private party had not already revealed.
cases: United States v. Reddick, 900 F.3d 636 (5th Cir. 2018)
United States v. Miller, 982 F.3d 412 (6th Cir. 2020)

sides.position: No. A hash-value match is not a valid private search, so law enforcement's visual examination of the matched file exceeds the scope of the private search and requires a warrant.
cases: United States v. Maher, 120 F.4th 297 (2d Cir. 2024)

entry.note: The Eleventh Circuit in Brillhart expressly declined to decide this question, and the records mention no pending en banc or certiorari petition.

opinions.cite: United States v. Richard Brillhart, No. 24-13232 (11th Cir. 2026)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: Our sister circuits are split over whether hash matching constitutes a valid private search.

opinions.cite: United States v. Maher, 120 F.4th 297 (2d Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: Three Courts of Appeals have considered that question, with the Fifth and Sixth Circuits answering it in the affirmative and the Ninth Circuit responding in the negati

entry.issue: Does the substantive-versus-clarifying test govern whether the Sentencing Commission's 2023 amendment to the compassionate-release Policy Statement (U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13) can apply to a sentence-reduction motion, so that an amendment treated as substantive cannot be applied to motions pending or filed before it took effect?

sides.position: The substantive-versus-clarifying test does not apply to sentence-modification proceedings, so the amended Policy Statement is not barred from applying to compassionate-release motions on that basis.
cases: United States v. Rutherford, 120 F.4th 360 (3d Cir. 2024)

sides.position: The amended Policy Statement is a substantive amendment that cannot be given retroactive effect to compassionate-release motions.
cases: United States v. Handlon, 97 F.4th 829, 833 (11th Cir. 2024)
United States v. Rutherford, 120 F.4th 360 (3d Cir. 2024)

opinions.cite: United States v. Daniel Rutherford, 120 F.4th 360 (3rd Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: The Third Circuit holds that the substantive-versus-clarifying test does not apply to a sentence modification, and it declines to follow Handlon.
opinions.quote: We part ways here with the Eleventh Circuit. United States v. Handlon, 97 F.4th 829, 833 (11th Cir. 2024) (holding that the amended Policy Statement is a substantive amendment that cannot be given retroactive effect).

entry.issue: Must the government prove actual force, violence, or intimidation to convict someone of attempted bank robbery under 18 U.S.C. § 2113(a)?

sides.position: Yes. The phrase "by force and violence, or by intimidation" modifies both "takes" and "attempts to take," so attempted bank robbery requires force, violence, or intimidation.
cases: Collier v. United States, 989 F.3d 212, 221 (2d Cir. 2021)
United States v. Vines, 134 F.4th 730 (3d Cir. 2025)
United States v. Bellew, 369 F.3d 450, 454 (5th Cir. 2004)
United States v. Thornton, 539 F.3d 741, 747 (7th Cir. 2008)
United States v. Brown, 412 F.2d 381 (8th Cir. 1969)
United States v. Armstrong, No. 21-11252 (11th Cir. Dec. 11, 2024)

sides.position: No. Attempted bank robbery under § 2113(a) does not require force, violence, or intimidation.
cases: United States v. McFadden, 739 F.2d 149, 151-52 (4th Cir. 1984)
United States v. Wesley, 417 F.3d 612, 618 (6th Cir. 2005)
United States v. Moore, 921 F.2d 207, 209 (9th Cir. 1990)

entry.note: The Second Circuit's 1976 Stallworth decision was dropped because the Second Circuit's later Collier decision and the Third Circuit's 2025 Vines decision place the Second Circuit on the force side, and the Armstrong record's reference to a "Jordan opinion" could not be matched to any case in the records.

opinions.cite: United States v. Ronald Vines, 134 F.4th 730 (3rd Cir. 2025)
opinions.takes: requires force or intimidation. The excerpt does not state the holding on this split in so many words, but the court reasons that a § 2113(d) attempt must incorporate § 2113(a)'s elements, which make it a crime of violence.
opinions.quote: But we have never addressed whether attempted bank robbery is, and our sister circuits are divided.

opinions.cite: United States v. John Armstrong, Jr., No. 21-11252 (11th Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: requires actual force, violence, or intimidation for attempted bank robbery (the majority's position, which the Jordan opinion says is the minority view)
opinions.quote: We recognize that our sister circuits are divided on this question.

entry.issue: When the government intentionally and unjustifiably intrudes into attorney-client communications about defense strategy, must the defendant show prejudice to establish a Sixth Amendment violation, and if prejudice is at issue, is it presumed or must the defendant prove it?

sides.position: Prejudice is presumed, but the presumption is rebuttable, so the government must disprove prejudice.
cases: United States v. Mastroianni, 749 F.2d 900 (1st Cir. 1984)
United States v. Danielson, 325 F.3d 1054 (9th Cir. 2003)
United States v. Irwin, 612 F.2d 1182 (9th Cir. 1980)

sides.position: Prejudice is conclusively presumed, so an intentional intrusion into defense strategy requires structural-error relief without any showing of prejudice.
cases: United States v. Levy, 577 F.2d 200 (3d Cir. 1978)
United States v. Shillinger, 70 F.3d 1132 (10th Cir. 1995)

sides.position: Defendant must show actual prejudice from the intrusion, and no presumption applies.
cases: ACLU Found. of S. Cal. v. Barr, 952 F.2d 457 (D.C. Cir. 1991)
United States v. Hohn, 123 F.4th 1084 (10th Cir. 2024)

opinions.cite: United States v. Hohn, 123 F.4th 1084 (10th Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: Defendant must show prejudice, and neither a rebuttable nor a conclusive presumption applies; the court rejects Shillinger's structural-error rule.
opinions.quote: We disagree with the minority of circuits that construe prejudice as a rebuttable presumption in the defendant’s favor.

entry.issue: Does the Florida Supreme Court's 2022 Somers decision, which held that aggravated assault cannot rest on reckless conduct, apply retroactively so that a pre-2022 Florida aggravated assault conviction based on reckless conduct does not qualify as an ACCA violent felony?

sides.position: Somers does not apply retroactively under Florida law, so a pre-2022 Florida aggravated assault conviction can still qualify as an ACCA predicate.
cases: United States v. Page, 123 F.4th 851 (7th Cir. 2024) (No. 21-3221)
United States v. Anderson, 99 F.4th ___ (7th Cir. 2024) (pin cites 1110–1114)

sides.position: Somers applies retroactively, so a pre-2022 Florida aggravated assault conviction based on reckless conduct does not qualify as an ACCA predicate because the statute did not reach reckless conduct at that time.
cases: Somers v. United States, 66 F.4th 890 (11th Cir. 2023)

entry.note: The records omit the reporter page for Anderson, so verify that citation before relying on it, and note that the Page dissent disputes the majority's treatment of this split and argues the split does not preclude plain error.

opinions.takes: The Seventh Circuit, as described in these excerpts, holds that Somers did not apply retroactively under Florida law. The excerpts come from a separate opinion that criticizes that approach and discusses the resulting split.
opinions.quote: Any error was "subject to reasonable dispute," Puckett, 556 U.S. at 135, as our majority opinion needed to distinguish a Florida Supreme Court decision on point and created a split with the Eleventh Circuit on an identical question.

opinions.takes: does not decide

entry.issue: Is evidence that an iMessage was transmitted over the Internet, without more, sufficient to prove that the communication actually crossed state lines for the interstate-commerce element of wire fraud?

sides.position: Use of the Internet, standing alone, does not establish that a transmission traveled across state lines in interstate commerce; the government must prove actual interstate crossing (construing § 1343 in Kieffer and Schaefer; Wright construes a different statute, 18 U.S.C. § 2252A(a)(1)).
cases: United States v. Kieffer, 681 F.3d 1143, 1153 (10th Cir. 2012)
United States v. Schaefer, 501 F.3d 1197, 1200–01 (10th Cir. 2007)
United States v. Wright, 625 F.3d 583, 590–95 (9th Cir. 2010)

sides.position: Contrary position on whether Internet transmission evidence suffices to establish interstate commerce. The excerpt does not spell out this holding; the opinion cites Haas as the opposing authority.
cases: United States v. Haas, 37 F.4th 1256, 1264–65 (7th Cir. 2022)

opinions.cite: United States v. O'Donovan, 126 F.4th 17 (1st Cir. 2025)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: There is a circuit split on the issue. See United States v. Haas, 37 F.4th 1256, 1264–65 (7th Cir. 2022).

entry.issue: Can police enter a home without a warrant under the emergency aid exception when no one reported an emergency and no relative or neighbor asked for help, but a hospital security guard reported that the resident's mother was missing?
entry.provision: U.S. Const. amend. IV; Brigham City v. Stuart, 547 U.S. 398 (2006)

sides.position: Warrantless emergency-aid entry requires an objectively reasonable basis, shown by facts such as a relative's or neighbor's request or signs of violence; a report from a hospital security guard that a person is unaccounted for does not suffice on these facts, and the entry here was unlawful.
cases: United States v. Giambro, 126 F.4th 46 (1st Cir. 2025)

sides.position: Emergency-aid entry is justified when police have reliable information that a person may be in medical distress, such as a concerned neighbor or doctor reporting that a person is unreachable, even without signs of violence inside the home.
cases: Gaetjens v. City of Loves Park, 4 F.4th 487 (7th Cir. 2021)
United States v. Maxwell, 85 F.4th 1243 (7th Cir. 2023) (en banc)

opinions.cite: United States v. Giambro, 126 F.4th 46 (1st Cir. 2025)
opinions.takes: The majority holds that the entry was not justified under the emergency aid exception and states that its holding creates no circuit split. The dissent asserts that the holding conflicts with Seventh Circuit emergency-aid decisions.
opinions.quote: The majority's holding also creates a circuit split.

entry.issue: Does the Foreign Commerce Clause give Congress broader power than the Interstate Commerce Clause to regulate the conduct of U.S. citizens abroad, so that 18 U.S.C. § 2423(c) can validly reach foreign sexual conduct by citizens?

sides.position: The Foreign Commerce Clause gives Congress greater authority to regulate foreign commerce than interstate commerce, and 18 U.S.C. § 2423(c) is a valid exercise of that power as applied to U.S. citizens abroad.
cases: United States v. Corrigan Clay, 128 F.4th 163 (3d Cir. 2025)
United States v. Pendleton, 658 F.3d 299 (3d Cir. 2011)
United States v. Clark, 435 F.3d 1100 (9th Cir. 2006)

sides.position: Upholding § 2423(c) through a channels-of-commerce theory is doubtful, because the statute punishes future foreign conduct divorced from travel and could permit federal prosecution of Americans for any offense committed abroad.
cases: United States v. Rife, 33 F.4th 838 (6th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Clark, 435 F.3d 1100, 1119 (9th Cir. 2006) (Ferguson, J., dissenting)
United States v. Durham, 902 F.3d (10th Cir. 2018) (Hartz, J., dissenting)

opinions.cite: United States v. Corrigan Clay, 128 F.4th 163 (3rd Cir. 2025)
opinions.takes: The Third Circuit holds that the Foreign Commerce Clause gives Congress broader power over foreign commerce, and that § 2423(c) is constitutional as applied here.
opinions.quote: Meanwhile, a circuit split has emerged regarding the scope of the Foreign Commerce Clause relative to its interstate counterpart.

entry.issue: Does a sentence imposed after the original sentence but before a subsequent resentencing count as a 'prior sentence' for criminal history points under U.S.S.G. § 4A1.1?

sides.position: A sentence imposed after the original sentence but before resentencing is a 'prior sentence' under § 4A1.1 and may be counted in the criminal history score.
cases: United States v. Garza, 127 F.4th 954 (5th Cir. 2025)
United States v. Hopper, 11 F.4th 561 (7th Cir. 2021)
United States v. Tidwell, 827 F.3d 761 (8th Cir. 2016)
United States v. Klump, 57 F.3d 801 (9th Cir. 1995)
United States v. Burke, 863 F.3d 1355 (11th Cir. 2017)

opinions.cite: United States v. Garza, 127 F.4th 954 (5th Cir. 2025)
opinions.takes: Sides with the majority of circuits and counts intervening sentences imposed before resentencing as prior sentences under § 4A1.1.
opinions.quote: The circuits are divided on this question.

entry.issue: Does the equipoise principle (that a conviction must be reversed when the evidence, viewed in the government's favor, gives equal or nearly equal support to guilt and innocence) remain part of federal sufficiency-of-the-evidence review, and if so, in what form?
entry.provision: Due Process Clause, U.S. Const. amend. V (sufficiency-of-the-evidence review)

sides.position: The equipoise principle remains a helpful tool in sufficiency review and is retained in some form; if the evidence is in equipoise after viewing it in the government's favor, a reasonable jury must entertain a reasonable doubt and the conviction must be reversed.
cases: United States v. Goldesberry, 128 F.4th 1183 (10th Cir. 2025)
United States v. Lovern, 590 F.3d 1095 (10th Cir. 2009)
United States v. Simon, 12 F.4th 1 (1st Cir. 2021)
United States v. Glenn, 312 F.3d 58 (2d Cir. 2002)

United States v. Johnson, 592 F.3d 749 (7th Cir. 2010)
Cosby v. Jones, 682 F.2d 1373 (11th Cir. 1982)

opinions.takes: Retains the equipoise principle as part of sufficiency review (the court's own position, drawing on Lovern).
opinions.quote: We note our sister circuits are divided on how the equipoise principle informs sufficiency review.

entry.issue: Does the Sixth Amendment Confrontation Clause apply to statements a prosecutor makes in closing argument?

sides.position: The Confrontation Clause applies to closing arguments. It is violated when a prosecutor tells the jury that an absent witness would have given inculpatory testimony.
cases: United States v. Molina-Guevara, 96 F.3d 698, 703 (3d Cir. 1996)

United States v. Miller, 982 F.3d 412, 439 (6th Cir. 2020)

opinions.cite: United States v. Lopez, 131 F.4th 1114 (10th Cir. 2025)
opinions.takes: does not decide

entry.issue: Under U.S.S.G. § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B), does the phrase "in connection with" require an articulable connection between the firearm and the other felony, excluding accidental or coincidental presence, or is it so vague and ambiguous that it should be read narrowly?

sides.position: The phrase "in connection with" is too vague and ambiguous to apply without a clear standard. Its drafting history, including Application Note 14 added to resolve a circuit disagreement over accidental or coincidental firearm presence, supports reading the enhancement narrowly.
cases: United States v. Perez, 5 F.4th 1 (3d Cir. 2021)

sides.position: The phrase "in connection with" has real boundaries drawn from Smith's construction of "in relation to." It requires an articulable connection between the firearm and the other felony, and the firearm's presence cannot be the result of accident or coincidence. Application Note 14 tracks Smith and is not ambiguous.

entry.issue: Is the D.C. Superior Court a "State court" under 28 U.S.C. § 2253(c)(1)(A), so that a D.C. prisoner's habeas appeal requires a certificate of appealability?

sides.position: The D.C. Superior Court is a "State court" under § 2253(c)(1)(A), so a D.C. prisoner needs a certificate of appealability to appeal a habeas denial.
cases: Garris v. Lindsay, 794 F.2d 722 (D.C. Cir. 1986)
Madley v. Crawford, 278 F.3d 1306 (11th Cir. 2001)
Wilson v. U.S. Parole Comm'n, 652 F.3d 348 (3d Cir. 2011)
Terry v. Deeboo, 473 F. App'x 282 (4th Cir. 2012)

sides.position: The D.C. Superior Court is not a "State court" under § 2253(c)(1)(A), so no certificate of appealability is required for a D.C. prisoner's habeas appeal.
cases: Eldridge v. Howard, 70 F.4th 543 (9th Cir. 2023)

opinions.cite: Clinton Eldridge v. Catricia Howard, 70 F.4th 543 (9th Cir. 2023)
opinions.takes: D.C. Superior Court is not a "State court" under § 2253(c)(1)(A); no certificate of appealability is required, which creates a split with the Eleventh Circuit's contrary reading in Madley.
opinions.quote: Madley reasoned that Garris's decision and Congress's later enactment of AEDPA means that "a court of the District is a state court for the purposes of [§ 2253(c)]."

entry.issue: Does the Fourth Amendment permit an officer to open a car door during a traffic stop without reasonable suspicion, or must the officer have reasonable suspicion to do so?
entry.provision: U.S. Const. amend. IV; Pennsylvania v. Mimms; Maryland v. Wilson

sides.position: Officers may open a car door during a traffic stop without reasonable suspicion, under Mimms and Wilson (the Fifth Circuit's version is limited to opening a door after an occupant is ordered out and claims inability to exit).
cases: United States v. Cotton, 721 F.2d 350 (11th Cir. 1983)
United States v. Meredith, 480 F.3d 366 (5th Cir. 2007)

sides.position: Officers may open a car door during a traffic stop only when they also have reasonable suspicion.

opinions.cite: United States v. Donte Dowdell, 70 F.4th 134 (3rd Cir. 2023)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: Whether an officer can open a car door during a traffic stop based on less than reasonable suspicion is an open question in our circuit. And our sister courts are divided on the question.

entry.issue: What standard of appellate review applies to a district court's denial of a Franks hearing on a challenge to a warrant affidavit?

sides.position: Review the district court's conclusions of law de novo and its factual findings for clear error when reviewing the denial of a Franks hearing.
cases: United States v. Sandalo, 70 F.4th 77 (2d Cir. 2023)
United States v. Rajaratnam, 719 F.3d 139, 156 n.19 (2d Cir. 2013)

opinions.cite: United States v. Domenico Sandalo, 70 F.4th 77 (2d Cir. 2023)
opinions.takes: Reviews conclusions of law de novo and factual findings for clear error; the excerpt does not say how the other side of the split reviews denials of Franks hearings.
opinions.quote: While there is a circuit split on the appropriate standard of review for the denial of a Franks hearing, see United States v. Rajaratnam, 719 F.3d 139, 156 n.19 (2d Cir. 2013), and there appears to be some confusion on the matter within our own circuit

entry.issue: Can a federal habeas petitioner use evidence outside the state-court record to establish cause for a procedural default under Martinez v. Ryan after Shinn v. Ramirez?

sides.position: Ramirez did not abrogate the circuit's rule that AEDPA does not bar factual development to excuse a procedural default, so new evidence may be considered for Martinez cause.
cases: Williams v. Superintendent Mahanoy SCI, 45 F.4th 713, 723 (3d Cir. 2022)

sides.position: Under Ramirez, new evidence may not be introduced to support a Martinez claim.
cases: Stokes v. Stirling, 64 F.4th 131, 136 (4th Cir. 2023)

opinions.cite: Mullis v. Lumpkin, 70 F.4th 906 (5th Cir. 2023)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: We acknowledge the circuit split on the question. Compare Williams v. Superintendent Mahanoy SCI, 45 F.4th 713, 723 (3d Cir. 2022) (holding that Ramirez did not abrogate the circuit’s holding that AEDPA does not forbid factual development regarding excusing procedural default), with Stokes v. Stirling, 64 F.4th 131, 136 (4th Cir. 2023) (concluding that Ramirez prohibits the introduction of new evidence in support of Martinez claims).

entry.issue: In a criminal forfeiture ancillary proceeding, does the government's interest in substitute property relate back to the date of the indictment or to the date of the underlying crime?

sides.position: The government's interest in substitute property relates back to the time of the indictment, not the time of the crime (the reading the parties agreed on, which the court did not endorse).
cases: United States v. Erpenbeck, 682 F.3d 472 (6th Cir. 2012)
United States v. Hallinan, 75 F.4th 148 (3d Cir. 2023)

cases: United States v. Erpenbeck, 682 F.3d 472 (6th Cir. 2012)
United States v. Hallinan, 75 F.4th 148 (3d Cir. 2023)

opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: (We take no position on whether that reading of the law is right; the circuits are split on that question. United States v. Erpenbeck, 682 F.3d 472, 477–78 (6th Cir. 2012) (Sutton, J.) (describing the circuit split).)

entry.issue: Can an anonymous tip that came through the 911 system, but whose caller did not use 911 in the way the tracing rationale assumes, still supply the reliability needed for reasonable suspicion for a stop under Navarette v. California?
entry.provision: U.S. Const. amend. IV; Navarette v. California, 572 U.S. 393 (2014)

sides.position: The 911 system's tracing capability is critical to the reliability of an anonymous tip. Where the caller does not use the 911 system (for example, by borrowing a stranger's phone), the Navarette 911 feature has much less force.
cases: United States v. Watson, 900 F.3d 892 (7th Cir. 2018)

sides.position: The caller's failure to use the 911 system is not detrimental to reliability, and the 911 feature can be distinguished on the facts, so the tip may still support reasonable suspicion.
cases: United States v. Wright, 74 F.4th 722 (5th Cir. 2023)

opinions.cite: United States v. Wright, 74 F.4th 722 (5th Cir. 2023)
opinions.takes: The majority takes the second position: the caller's failure to use the 911 system is not detrimental, and the majority distinguishes Watson.
opinions.quote: Although the majority seeks to differentiate countervailing authority, it discredits the circuit split recognizing the critical importance of the 911 system’s tracing abilities.

entry.issue: After Kisor v. Wilkie, must a federal court find the Sentencing Guidelines genuinely ambiguous, after exhausting traditional tools of construction, before deferring to the Guidelines commentary under Stinson v. United States?
entry.provision: U.S.S.G. commentary and application notes (e.g., U.S.S.G. § 1B1.7, § 2G2.2(b)(5), § 4B1.2 cmt. n.1); Stinson v. United States, 508 U.S. 36 (1993); Kisor v. Wilkie, 588 U.S. 558 (2019)

sides.position: Kisor applies to Guidelines commentary. A court may defer to the commentary only if the guideline is genuinely ambiguous after traditional tools of construction are exhausted, and only if the commentary's reading is reasonable and entitled to controlling weight.

United States v. Riccardi, 989 F.3d 476 (6th Cir. 2021)
United States v. Castillo, 69 F.4th 648 (9th Cir. 2023)
United States v. Scheu, 83 F.4th 1124 (9th Cir. 2023)
United States v. Mendonsa, No. 25-1517 (9th Cir. 2026)
United States v. Dupree, 57 F.4th 1269 (11th Cir. 2023) (en banc)

sides.position: Kisor does not modify Stinson. Guidelines commentary keeps its Stinson deference and does not require a prior finding that the guideline is genuinely ambiguous.
cases: United States v. Moses, 23 F.4th 347 (4th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Vargas, 74 F.4th 673 (5th Cir. 2023) (en banc)
United States v. Johnson, 104 F.4th 662 (7th Cir. 2024)
United States v. Smith, 989 F.3d 575 (7th Cir. 2021)
United States v. Maloid, 71 F.4th 795 (10th Cir. 2023)

entry.note: The records conflict on the Fourth Circuit (Campbell, 2022, lists it on the Kisor side, while Moses, 2022, and later decisions list it on the Stinson side), so this entry follows Moses and the later decisions; verify before relying on it. The Eighth Circuit (Rivera, 2023) has expressly declined to decide the question.

opinions.cite: United States v. Mendonsa, No. 25-1517 (9th Cir. 2026)
opinions.takes: Applies the Kisor framework, following Castillo (9th Cir. 2023).
opinions.quote: Although the circuits disagree over the deference owed to the Guidelines commentary after Kisor, this court applies the Kisor framework.

opinions.cite: United States v. Christopher Johnson, 104 F.4th 662 (7th Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: Kisor does not modify Stinson; this court follows its earlier decision in White, holding that Kisor does not change the deference owed to Guidelines commentary.
opinions.quote: Our sister circuits are divided as to whether Kisor's prerequisites for the deference owed to agency interpretations also apply to the deference owed to guidelines commentary.

opinions.cite: United States v. Junaid Gulzar, 92 F.4th 684 (7th Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: He asks us to conclude that Kisor overruled the Supreme Court's earlier decision in Stinson, 508 U.S. at 45, an issue presently subject to a circuit split.

opinions.cite: United States v. Joshua Scheu, No. 22-10044 (9th Cir. 2023)
opinions.takes: Follows the Kisor-applies position (adopted in Castillo, which Scheu reaffirms). Scheu itself does not decide the broader post-Kisor question of how much weight commentary receives, because it holds the Guideline unambiguous.
opinions.quote: Since Kisor was decided, a circuit split has arisen over whether this more limited deference should apply to the Sentencing Guidelines commentary and application notes.

opinions.cite: United States v. Remberto Rivera, 76 F.4th 1085 (8th Cir. 2023)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: While there is circuit disagreement on the deference to be afforded the Guidelines' commentary, the weight of authority may suggest that Kisor undermines the Court's decision in Mendoza-Figueroa.

opinions.cite: United States v. Joshua Scheu, 83 F.4th 1124 (9th Cir. 2023)
opinions.takes: Adopts the Kisor side: the Ninth Circuit agrees that the more demanding Kisor standard applies to Guidelines commentary, following its earlier decision in Castillo.
opinions.quote: Since Kisor was decided, a circuit split has arisen over whether this more limited deference should apply to the Sentencing Guidelines commentary and application notes.

entry.issue: Does a due process violation from the government's selective grant or withholding of immunity require proof that the prosecutor subjectively intended to distort the fact-finding process, or is it enough that the immunity decision in fact distorted fact-finding?
entry.provision: U.S. Const. amend. V (due process); 18 U.S.C. §§ 6002, 6003(b)

sides.position: Due process is violated only if the government immunizes or withholds immunity from witnesses with the intention of distorting the fact-finding process (the Davis standard), with no further requirement of subjective intent.
cases: United States v. Davis, 845 F.3d 282 (7th Cir. 2016)
United States v. Newton, 76 F.4th 662 (7th Cir. 2023)

sides.position: In addition to distorting the fact-finding process, the prosecutor must have subjectively intended to cause that manipulation.
cases: United States v. Newton, 76 F.4th 662 (7th Cir. 2023)

opinions.cite: United States v. Angelita Newton, 76 F.4th 662 (7th Cir. 2023)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: The parties also disagree about which side of a circuit split we have come down on in regard to whether, in addition to distorting the fact-finding process, the prosecutor must have subjectively intended to cause such manipulation.

entry.issue: When a defendant is convicted of conspiracy under 18 U.S.C. § 1594(c), is the base offense level under U.S.S.G. § 2G1.1(a) set by the statute of conviction or by the conduct the conspiracy aimed to commit?

sides.position: Base offense level is determined by the offense of conviction (§ 1594(c) conspiracy, so the 'otherwise' level of 14 applies), not by the underlying conduct the conspiracy targeted.
cases: United States v. Wei Lin, 841 F.3d 823 (9th Cir. 2016)

sides.position: Base offense level may be set by the conduct the conspiracy aimed to commit (through § 1B1.3 cmt. n.7), so the § 1591(b)(1) level of 34 can apply to a § 1594(c) conspiracy conviction.
cases: United States v. Sims, 957 F.3d 362 (3d Cir. 2020)
United States v. Carter, 960 F.3d 1007 (8th Cir. 2020)

opinions.cite: United States v. Samuel Nichols, 77 F.4th 490 (7th Cir. 2023)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: Since Nichols's sentencing, circuits have split as to how § 2G1.1 should be applied to those convicted of violating § 1594(c).

entry.issue: In a federal criminal case under CIPA, must the government formally invoke the state-secrets privilege through the head of the department with control over the matter (or its political head), as Reynolds requires, or may a lower-level official invoke it?
entry.provision: Classified Information Procedures Act, 18 U.S.C. App. 3 § 4; United States v. Reynolds, 345 U.S. 1 (1953)

sides.position: Formal invocation of the state-secrets privilege requires a declaration by the head of the department with control over the matter (or its political head), as Reynolds requires, even in criminal cases under CIPA.

United States v. Stewart, 590 F.3d 93 (2d Cir. 2009)
United States v. Alahmedalabdaloklah, 94 F.4th 782 (9th Cir. 2023)
United States v. Alahmedalabdaloklah, No. 18-10435 (9th Cir. 2024)

sides.position: An agency head need not personally invoke the state-secrets privilege in criminal matters under CIPA; a lower-level official's invocation can suffice.
cases: United States v. Rosen, 557 F.3d 192 (4th Cir. 2009)
United States v. El-Mezain, 664 F.3d 467 (5th Cir. 2011)

opinions.quote: Other circuit courts are divided on this issue.

opinions.takes: Requires formal invocation by the department head; the Ninth Circuit adheres to its prior CIPA decisions and to Reynolds, although it excuses the government's noncompliance in this case.

entry.issue: Can 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1), the federal felon-in-possession ban, be unconstitutional under the Second Amendment as applied to some felons, and if so, how should courts decide that?

sides.position: Section 922(g)(1) is constitutional as applied to all felons. Felon disarmament is consistent with the historical tradition, so courts need not conduct an individualized or as-applied inquiry, and pre-Bruen precedent upholding the statute remains good law.
cases: United States v. Hunt, 123 F.4th 697 (4th Cir. 2024)
United States v. Jackson, 110 F.4th 1120 (8th Cir. 2024)
United States v. Duarte, 137 F.4th 743 (9th Cir. 2025) (en banc)
Vincent v. Bondi, 127 F.4th 1263 (10th Cir. 2025)
United States v. Dubois, 139 F.4th 887 (11th Cir. 2025)

sides.position: Section 922(g)(1) may be unconstitutional as applied to some felons, so an as-applied challenge is available. Courts assess whether the defendant's predicate offense is relevantly similar to a historically disqualifying crime, looking to dangerousness, and the predicate must be punishable by more than one year of imprisonment. Classification as a felony alone is not enough.
cases: Range v. Att'y Gen., 124 F.4th 218 (3d Cir. 2024) (en banc)
United States v. Diaz, 116 F.4th 458 (5th Cir. 2024)
United States v. Mitchell, 160 F.4th 177 (5th Cir. 2025)
United States v. Squire, No. 25-30324 (5th Cir. 2026)
United States v. Williams, 113 F.4th 637 (6th Cir. 2024)
United States v. Martin, No. 24-3750, 2025 WL 1913185 (6th Cir. July 11, 2025)
United States v. Simmons, 150 F.4th 126 (2d Cir. 2025)
United States v. Watson, 171 F.4th 1012 (7th Cir. 2026)

entry.note: The records disagree on where the 2d, 5th, 9th and 10th Circuits sit, so I used each circuit's own most recent opinion (Simmons for the 2d, Squire and Mitchell for the 5th, Duarte en banc for the 9th, Vincent for the 10th), and the Fifth Circuit's Allred decision (July 2026) applies a categorical approach to individual history, which should be checked against Squire and Mancilla before relying on this placement.

opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: We note that our sister circuits are split on the question of whether individuals with felony convictions are among "the people" protected by the Second Amendment, with most circuits holding that they are.

opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: Our sister circuits are deeply divided on whether pre-Bruen precedents upholding section 922(g)(1) remain good law and on whether lifetime felon disarmament is constitutional absent some individualized inquiry into whether the individual felon is dangerous.

opinions.takes: Categorical, felony-by-felony approach (the majority follows Kimble and applies it to § 922(g)(9)); the individualized-assessment view appears only in Judge Graves's concurrence.
opinions.quote: "There is already a robust circuit split" regarding how courts should consider as-applied challenges to § 922(g)(1).

opinions.quote: An entrenched circuit split has now emerged about its proper application.

opinions.cite: United States v. Mitchell, No. 24-60607 (5th Cir. 2025)
opinions.takes: Recognizes that § 922(g)(1) may be unconstitutional as applied to some felons, but is bound by Diaz and rejects the as-applied challenge in this case under that precedent.
opinions.quote: An entrenched circuit split has now emerged about its proper application.

opinions.takes: The excerpts do not state the holding, but the reasoning favors the predicate-by-predicate, as-applied side, which is opposed to the categorical rule adopted by the sister circuits listed above.

opinions.takes: does not decide

entry.issue: Does a state-law drug offense count as a 'controlled substance offense' under U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) only if it matches the federal definition of a controlled substance?

sides.position: Yes. A prior state drug conviction qualifies only if the substance is also controlled under federal law (federal-definition or categorical approach). The records describe this as the majority side, with seven circuits in total. Only four are named here: the 1st, 2d, 5th, and 9th. The other three are not identified in the records.
cases: United States v. Townsend, 897 F.3d 66 (2d Cir. 2018)
United States v. Gibson, 55 F.4th 153 (2d Cir. 2022)
United States v. Chaires, 88 F.4th 172 (2d Cir. 2023)

United States v. Fulcar, No. 24-1524 (1st Cir. 2026)
United States v. Chaney, No. 23-30454 (5th Cir. 2026)

sides.position: No. A state drug conviction can qualify without being measured against the federal definition (state-dependent approach). The records describe this as a three-circuit minority. Only two are named here: the 3d and 6th. The third is not identified in the records.

United States v. T'Shaun Omar Jones, 81 F.4th 591 (6th Cir. 2023)

opinions.quote: In the meantime, every other circuit to consider the issue post-Trammel has rejected the joint participant exception to the spousal testimonial privilege.

entry.issue: Does fugitive tolling suspend a federal supervised release term while the releasee is absconding from supervision?

sides.position: Fugitive tolling applies: the supervised release term is suspended while the releasee is a fugitive.
cases: United States v. Barinas, 865 F.3d 99 (2d Cir. 2017)
United States v. Island, 916 F.3d 249 (3d Cir. 2019)
United States v. Buchanan, 638 F.3d 448 (4th Cir. 2011)
United States v. Murguia-Oliveros, 421 F.3d 951 (9th Cir. 2005)

sides.position: Fugitive tolling does not apply: the supervised release term keeps running while the releasee is a fugitive.
cases: United States v. Hernandez-Ferrer, 599 F.3d 63 (1st Cir. 2010)
United States v. Talley, 83 F.4th 1296 (11th Cir. 2023)

entry.note: The Fifth Circuit noted this four-to-two split in United States v. Swick, 137 F.4th 336 (5th Cir. 2025) but did not take a side, so the question remains open in that circuit, and the records mention no pending en banc or certiorari petition.

opinions.cite: United States v. Swick, 137 F.4th 336 (5th Cir. 2025)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: We begin by explaining there is currently a four-to-two circuit split on whether fugitive tolling exists in the supervised release context: the Second, Third, Fourth, and Ninth Circuits hold that it does; the First and Eleventh Circuits hold that it does not.

opinions.cite: United States v. James Reginald Talley, 83 F.4th 1296 (11th Cir. 2023)
opinions.takes: No fugitive tolling; the court joins the First Circuit and holds the term of supervised release is not tolled by fugitive status.
opinions.quote: The circuits are divided over the application of “fugitive tolling” to terms of supervised release.

entry.issue: Which constitutional provision supplies a criminal defendant's right to be present at sentencing: the Due Process Clause or the Confrontation Clause?
entry.provision: U.S. Const. amend. V (Due Process Clause); U.S. Const. amend. VI (Confrontation Clause); FED. R. CRIM. P. 32(i)(2)

sides.position: The right to be present at sentencing derives from the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment.
cases: United States v. Diggles, 957 F.3d 551 (5th Cir. 2020) (en banc)
United States v. Montoya, 82 F.4th 640 (9th Cir. 2023)

sides.position: The right to be present at sentencing derives from the Confrontation Clause of the Sixth Amendment.
cases: United States v. Ferrario-Pozzi, 368 F.3d 5 (1st Cir. 2004)
United States v. Townsend, 33 F.3d 1230 (10th Cir. 1994)

opinions.cite: United States v. Cynthia Montoya, 82 F.4th 640 (9th Cir. 2023)
opinions.takes: Due Process Clause for proceedings lacking testimony, which includes most sentencings; the Confrontation Clause may also apply in the rare sentencing proceedings that include evidence or witness testimony.
opinions.quote: The Supreme Court has not directly addressed the constitutional basis for a defendant’s right to be present during sentencing, and the circuits are split on the basis for this right.

entry.issue: Does the First Step Act's retroactivity provision (§ 404) cover a defendant whose sentence for a covered offense was imposed before the Act's effective date but later vacated, or does the earlier sentence count as 'a sentence' imposed as a matter of historical fact, barring relief?
entry.provision: First Step Act of 2018, Pub. L. 115-391, § 404

sides.position: A sentence imposed before the Act's effective date counts as 'a sentence' as a matter of historical fact even if it was later vacated, so the defendant is not eligible for § 404 relief.
cases: United States v. Jackson, 995 F.3d 511 (6th Cir. 2021)
United States v. Carpenter, 80 F.4th 790 (6th Cir. 2023)

sides.position: A sentence that was vacated does not bar § 404 relief, so the defendant may seek a reduced sentence under the Act's retroactivity provision.
cases: United States v. Mitchell, 38 F.4th 382 (3d Cir. 2022)
United States v. Merrell, 36 F.4th 571 (9th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Bethea, 841 F. App'x 544 (4th Cir. 2021)

opinions.cite: United States v. Timothy Carpenter, 80 F.4th 790 (6th Cir. 2023)
opinions.takes: The Sixth Circuit, through Jackson and this denial of en banc review, holds that a pre-Act sentence counts as 'a sentence' even if vacated, so the defendant is not eligible for § 404 relief.
opinions.quote: Jackson also splits from all our sister circuits to have reached the question.

entry.issue: Does the limited confrontation right in Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 32.1(b)(2)(C) apply to the sentencing phase of a supervised release revocation hearing, or only to the phase deciding whether the releasee violated the conditions?

sides.position: Rule 32.1(b)(2)(C)'s confrontation right applies to the sentencing phase of revocation proceedings.
cases: United States v. Combs, 36 F.4th 502 (4th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Garcia-Oquendo, No. 24-1666 (1st Cir. 2025)

sides.position: Rule 32.1(b)(2)(C)'s confrontation right does not apply to the sentencing phase of revocation proceedings; due process requires no greater protection at that stage.
cases: United States v. Ruby, 706 F.3d 1221 (10th Cir. 2013)
United States v. Busey, 11 F.4th 664 (8th Cir. 2021)
United States v. Williams, 847 F.3d 251 (5th Cir. 2017)

entry.note: United States v. Navarro-Santisteban, 83 F.4th 44 (1st Cir. 2023), addresses a separate question about whether hearsay is barred at the revocation sentencing phase, so it is not merged into this entry and should be checked separately.

opinions.cite: United States v. Garcia-Oquendo, No. 24-1666 (1st Cir. 2025)
opinions.takes: The First Circuit holds that Rule 32.1(b)(2)(C)'s limited confrontation right applies to the entirety of the revocation proceeding, including the sentencing phase, thereby siding with the Fourth Circuit and rejecting the Tenth Circuit's contrary holding in Ruby.
opinions.quote: Other circuits have split on the issue.

opinions.cite: United States v. Navarro-Santisteban, 83 F.4th 44 (1st Cir. 2023)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: See United States v. Torres-Santana, 991 F.3d 257, 265 (1st Cir. 2021) (recognizing circuit split on the issue and declining to resolve the legal question where facts made it unnecessary to do so).

entry.issue: Does 'loss' under the Sentencing Guidelines' fraud table (U.S.S.G. § 2B1.1(b)(1)) include intended loss, or is it limited to actual loss?
entry.provision: U.S.S.G. § 2B1.1(b)(1) and its commentary, Application Note (A)

sides.position: 'Loss' includes intended loss. Courts defer to the § 2B1.1 commentary directing use of the greater of actual or intended loss, so intended loss can raise the offense level.
cases: United States v. Gadson, 77 F.4th 16 (1st Cir. 2023)
United States v. You, 74 F.4th 378 (6th Cir. 2023)
United States v. Lee, 77 F.4th 565 (7th Cir. 2023)
United States v. Verdeza, 69 F.4th 780 (11th Cir. 2023)
United States v. Tellez Crespo, 86 F.4th 1148 (6th Cir. 2023)
United States v. Nock, 148 F.4th 607 (8th Cir. 2025)
United States v. Holthaus, 486 F.3d 451 (8th Cir. 2007)
United States v. Currie, No. 25-2666, 25-3141 (8th Cir. 2026)

sides.position: 'Loss' is limited to actual loss. The Guideline text does not reach intended loss, and the commentary does not control.
cases: United States v. Banks, 55 F.4th 246 (3d Cir. 2022)

entry.note: Currie reports that the Supreme Court has granted certiorari in Beaird v. United States on this split, so the law may change; check the current status of Beaird before relying on this entry.

opinions.cite: United States v. Latroy Currie, No. 25-2666, 25-3141 (8th Cir. 2026)
opinions.takes: defers to the commentary and follows Nock; the court holds that intended loss may be considered and does not resolve the split, noting the Supreme Court has granted certiorari in Beaird v. United States
opinions.quote: Supreme Court has granted certiorari to consider a circuit split on this issue.

opinions.cite: United States v. Yanier Tellez Crespo, 86 F.4th 1148 (6th Cir. 2023)
opinions.takes: Follows the intended-loss view under binding Sixth Circuit precedent (United States v. You), while noting that the opposing reading may be correct and not deciding the question on the merits.
opinions.quote: The Third Circuit, we note, has held otherwise.

entry.issue: For a Guidelines career offender or controlled substance offense enhancement based on a prior drug conviction, must the court apply the drug definitions in effect when the prior offense occurred, or those in effect at federal sentencing?
entry.provision: U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) (controlled substance offense) and § 4B1.1 (career offender); see also U.S.S.G. § 1B1.11

sides.position: Time of the prior conviction: the prior offense is measured against the controlled-substance definitions in effect when the defendant was convicted of it (the 8th Circuit applies this to the prior state sentencing), so a substance later removed from federal control still counts.
cases: United States v. Clark, 46 F.4th 404 (6th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Perez, 46 F.4th 691 (8th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Henderson, 11 F.4th 713 (8th Cir. 2021)
United States v. Bailey, 37 F.4th 467 (8th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Gordon, 111 F.4th 899 (8th Cir. 2024)
United States v. Dubois, 94 F.4th 1284 (11th Cir. 2024)

sides.position: Time of federal sentencing: the prior offense is measured against the controlled-substance definitions in effect at federal sentencing, so a substance later removed from federal control no longer qualifies.
cases: United States v. Abdulaziz, 998 F.3d 519 (1st Cir. 2021)
United States v. Minor, 121 F.4th 1085 (5th Cir. 2024)

entry.note: The Supreme Court had not resolved the split as of these opinions, and the placement of the 2d, 4th, and 9th Circuits is unverified because it appears only in an inferred mapping from the Minor dissent, so check each circuit's current law before relying on it.

opinions.cite: United States v. Minor, 121 F.4th 1085 (5th Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: time-of-sentencing (the majority adopts this rule and states the court 'has now picked a side' while awaiting Supreme Court resolution)
opinions.quote: As the majority points out, the circuits are deeply split over whether the correct approach to applying the § 4B1.1 enhancement is time-ofconviction or time-of-sentencing.

opinions.cite: United States v. Nethaniah Gordon, 111 F.4th 899 (8th Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: The Eighth Circuit follows the first position, holding that the state-law definition at the time of the prior state sentencing controls and that Gordon's prior Iowa marijuana conviction qualifies.
opinions.quote: There is a circuit split on this Guidelines issue as well, but the Supreme Court has not addressed either issue.

opinions.cite: United States v. Andre Michael Dubois, 94 F.4th 1284 (11th Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: Time of the prior state conviction controls; the court adopts a time-of-state-conviction rule.
opinions.quote: Our sister circuits are split on this timing question.

entry.issue: May a district court, when revoking supervised release under 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e), consider the retribution factor in 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a)(2)(A) (the need for the sentence to reflect the seriousness of the offense and promote respect for the law)?

sides.position: A court may consider retribution (§ 3553(a)(2)(A)) when revoking supervised release, as the Sixth Circuit held in United States v. Lewis and the panel's amended order in this case. The dissents say this places the Sixth Circuit at the extreme of a split.
cases: United States v. Lewis, 498 F.3d 393 (6th Cir. 2007)
United States v. Esteras, 95 F.4th 454 (6th Cir. 2024)

sides.position: A court may not consider retribution (§ 3553(a)(2)(A)) when revoking supervised release. The excerpts describe this as the position of other circuits but do not name them.

opinions.cite: United States v. Edgardo Esteras, 95 F.4th 454 (6th Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: The Sixth Circuit permits consideration of retribution when revoking supervised release (Lewis; the amended panel order), and the court denied rehearing en banc over dissents.
opinions.quote: place the Sixth Circuit at the extreme of a circuit split, allowing our district courts expressly to punish defendants for violations of supervised release.

entry.issue: Can a district court reduce, under § 404 of the First Step Act, the sentence for a non-covered offense that was grouped or packaged with a covered crack cocaine offense?

sides.position: Yes. A court may reduce a non-covered sentence that was grouped or packaged with a covered offense, because the First Step Act does not exclude grouped non-covered offenses.
cases: United States v. Richardson, 96 F.4th 659 (4th Cir. 2024)
United States v. Hudson, 967 F.3d 605 (7th Cir. 2020)
United States v. Curtis, 66 F.4th 690 (7th Cir. 2023)
United States v. Spencer, 998 F.3d 843 (8th Cir. 2021)
United States v. Gordon (6th Cir. 2025)

sides.position: No. The First Step Act lets a court reduce only the sentence for the covered offense, and the sentencing-package doctrine does not supply the express statutory authority needed to modify a non-covered sentence.
cases: United States v. Young, 998 F.3d 43 (2d Cir. 2021)
United States v. Gladney, 44 F.4th 1253 (10th Cir. 2022)
United States v. Baptiste, 834 F. App'x 547 (11th Cir. 2020)

entry.note: The Sixth Circuit's Gordon decision (2025) is the most recent and controls within that circuit, but the records give inconsistent docket numbers (23-1070 versus 23-1050/1069/1070/1071) and no reporter cite, so verify the citation before relying on it.

opinions.cite: United States v. John Gordon, No. 23-1070 (6th Cir. 2025)
opinions.takes: The Sixth Circuit adopts the sentencing-package interpretation, finding the reasoning of the courts permitting such reductions more persuasive, and remands to decide whether the doctrine applies on these facts.
opinions.quote: Although some circuits disagree on this issue, we find the reasoning of courts adopting a sentencing-package interpretation more persuasive.

opinions.cite: United States v. Nathaniel Richardson, Jr., 96 F.4th 659 (4th Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: Permits the reduction for a grouped noncovered offense, following the Seventh Circuit's reasoning in Hudson. The excerpts do not name the contrary circuits, so the opposing side is not shown.
opinions.quote: we agree with the reasoning of the Seventh Circuit that the First Step Act does not exclude noncovered offenses because doing so would impose an "extra-textual limitation" since the statute did not constrain its application to grouped and noncovered offenses.

entry.issue: Does Virginia v. Black comprehensively define the category of unprotected true threats, so that a threat is unprotected only if it targets a particular individual or group of individuals?
entry.provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (Free Speech Clause)

sides.position: Black comprehensively defines the category of true threats, so a communication is unprotected only if it threatens a particular individual or group of individuals.
cases: United States v. Dutcher, 851 F.3d 757, 761 (7th Cir. 2017)
United States v. Floyd, 458 F.3d 844, 848 (8th Cir. 2006)
United States v. Bagdasarian, 652 F.3d 1113, 1116 (9th Cir. 2011)
United States v. Wheeler, 776 F.3d 736, 743 (10th Cir. 2015)

sides.position: Black does not exhaustively define true threats; the Supreme Court said the category 'encompass[es]' such statements but did not limit it to them.
cases: United States v. Fleury, 20 F.4th 1353, 1373 (11th Cir. 2021)

opinions.cite: United States v. Davit Davitashvili, 97 F.4th 104 (3rd Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: does not decide
opinions.quote: But other courts of appeals have read Black as comprehensively defining the category of true threats.

entry.issue: Does a prisoner who wins resentencing relief get to challenge an undisturbed underlying conviction in a later habeas petition without that petition being treated as second or successive under 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)?

sides.position: Yes. A resentencing that legally invalidates or alters the sentence creates a new judgment, so the prisoner may raise challenges to the undisturbed conviction in a later petition, and the petition is not second or successive. The imposition of a new sentence alone is not the test.
cases: Donovan v. Massachusetts Parole Board, No. 23-1810 (1st Cir. 2025)
Johnson v. United States, 623 F.3d 41 (2d Cir. 2010)
Lesko v. Secretary Pennsylvania Department of Corrections, 34 F.4th 211 (3d Cir. 2022)
United States v. Hill, 98 F.4th 473 (3d Cir. 2024)
In re Edwards, 98 F.4th 425 (3d Cir. 2024)
Buenrostro v. United States, 895 F.3d 1160 (9th Cir. 2018)

sides.position: No. A resentencing creates a new judgment only as to the amended count or sentence. It does not reopen an undisturbed conviction, so later challenges to that conviction are second or successive under § 2244(b).
cases: In re Lampton, 667 F.3d 585 (5th Cir. 2012)
Suggs v. United States, 705 F.3d 279 (7th Cir. 2013)
Burks v. Raemisch, 680 F. App'x 686 (10th Cir. 2017)

entry.note: The records mention no pending en banc or certiorari petition, but the Donovan dissent argues the majority wrongly discounted Suggs and Burks, so the split may still be contested and should be checked for later developments.

opinions.cite: Donovan v. Massachusetts Parole Board, No. 23-1810 (1st Cir. 2025)
opinions.takes: The majority adopts the position that a resentencing can create a new judgment permitting renewed challenges to the conviction. The dissent says the majority discounted Suggs and Burks, which places the majority on the other side of the split.
opinions.quote: The majority is simply wrong to discount Suggs and Burks for relying on pre-Magwood circuit precedent; those courts did so precisely because Magwood declined to resolve the issue.

opinions.cite: United States v. Carlos Hill, 98 F.4th 473 (3rd Cir. 2024)
opinions.takes: Follows the majority interpretation: a prisoner who receives relief as to his sentence may raise a challenge to an undisturbed conviction in a second-in-time petition.
opinions.quote: The Lesko panel acknowledged that a circuit split exists after Magwood but sided with the majority of circuits that have considered the issue:

sides.position: First Step Act § 403(a) applies at resentencing following vacatur where the Act was enacted after the original sentencing but before resentencing (position as described in Eldridge n.17 as one side of a noted circuit split; the excerpts do not state the holding)

entry.issue: Is a pretrial bail hearing a critical stage at which the Sixth Amendment right to counsel attaches?

sides.position: A bail hearing is a critical stage, so the accused has a right to counsel at it.
cases: Higazy v. Templeton, 505 F.3d 161 (2d Cir. 2007)
Betschart v. Washington County Circuit Court Judges, 103 F.4th 607 (9th Cir. 2024)

United States v. Braunstein, 281 F.3d 982 (9th Cir. 2002)
